lesson.title: Slavery by Another Name: The Black Codes of 1865 and 1866
lesson.summary: Passed by Southern legislatures under Andrew Johnson's lenient Reconstruction plan, the Black Codes used the language of law to reimpose many of the controls of slavery on newly freed people, and their harshness helped push Congress toward Radical Reconstruction.
lesson.body:
Slavery had barely ended before Southern state legislatures began looking for ways to control Black labor and movement without technically owning people. Under President Andrew Johnson's lenient Reconstruction policy, which asked little of the reorganized Southern state governments beyond ratifying the Thirteenth Amendment and repudiating secession, Mississippi and South Carolina passed the first Black Codes in late 1865, and other former Confederate states quickly followed with their own versions through 1866.

These laws did not invent new tools of racial control so much as adapt old ones. The antebellum South had long regulated enslaved people's lives through slave codes and armed patrols that controlled movement, required written passes to travel, and punished unauthorized gatherings. The Black Codes drew on that same legal tradition and applied it to people who were now, on paper, free citizens, showing how deeply the assumptions behind slavery persisted even after the institution itself was abolished.

The specific provisions varied by state but followed a common pattern. Vagrancy laws allowed local authorities to arrest any Black person found without proof of employment and force them into labor, often for a white employer who paid their fine. Many states required freedpeople to sign annual labor contracts, and breaking one could mean arrest. Mississippi restricted Black residents from renting land or practicing certain trades outside agriculture, aiming to keep freedpeople tied to plantation labor. Apprenticeship laws allowed courts to take Black children from their parents and bind them into unpaid labor for white employers, often the very families who had previously enslaved them, under the guise of vocational training. Other provisions banned interracial marriage, restricted Black gun ownership, and imposed curfews enforced by all white local police.

The vagrancy and criminal provisions in particular exploited a loophole left open by the Thirteenth Amendment itself, which had abolished slavery and involuntary servitude except as punishment for a crime. By criminalizing unemployment, minor offenses, and ordinary movement, Southern lawmakers created a legal pipeline that funneled Black men and women into forced labor through the criminal justice system, an arrangement that would evolve over subsequent decades into the convict leasing system, in which prisoners, overwhelmingly Black, were leased out to plantations, mines, and railroads under conditions often as brutal as slavery itself.

News of the Black Codes traveled quickly to the North and produced real outrage, providing Republicans in Congress with concrete evidence that Johnson's lenient Reconstruction plan was allowing the South to reconstruct slavery under a new legal name. That outrage fed directly into Congress's decision in December 1865 to refuse Southern states' elected representatives, its passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1866, and ultimately its decision in 1867 to impose Radical Reconstruction and military oversight on the South, a far more interventionist policy than anything Johnson had planned.
